Editor’s note: This article discusses mature themes.

We’re wasting an awful lot of time talking about “consent” and sexual regret right now, thanks to a young woman suing several men she had group sex with at Cornell University, when we really should be talking about the powerful effect of not consuming hard drugs.

TMZ this week published newly revealed text messages between who we now know as Cornell’s “Jane Doe” and one of the Chi Phi fraternity members she accused of gang raping her two years ago. “[I]f you have any regrets or anything you want to talk about i am always here to talk about it cause that was a lot,” Doe wrote in one of the messages. “i really do love u and matt and i promise i wont get quiet and weird w u like i did last time.” The name Matt appears to be a reference to another one of the men she is accusing, though public evidence shows she justified and defended their sexual engagement in a similar message to him as well.

And here’s the truly relevant message she sent to one of the accused, as reported by TMZ: “ps. i’m not sure if u remember but i did ket off your d–k at some point?” she wrote. “[A]nd i honestly think that was one of the most insane/jaw dropping moments of the night.” Her use of the word “ket” is apparently a reference to the drug ketamine, which her own lawsuit indicates she snorted an alarming amount of on the night in question.

That brings us to where we should have been all along. College students, ladies in particular, don’t do hard drugs. Especially when it involves a group of men.

We don’t know yet what exactly happened in October 2024 at the Chi Phi fraternity house with Jane Doe. We probably never will. But all public evidence currently indicates a 20-year-old woman got drunk at a sorority house, went to a couple of bars, then went to a frat house where she met a male friend and initially agreed to a threesome that ultimately included drugs and may have included other men.

No one begrudges a college student, whether male or female, drinking underage. If she’s legally old enough to have died for her country, she can have as many drinks as she wants (so long as she’s not caught). But drinking comes with consequences. Everything does. That includes consuming hard drugs.

Jane Doe reportedly said in other text messages days after the night of partying that she could only “sleep and cry all day.” Without concluding whether she was raped, that testimony isn’t discernibly different from any person who has done hard drugs and is on a come-down. Drugs like ketamine create a hyper sense of euphoria while it’s in the system. And once it’s gone, the user crashes. Depression and anxiety are normal. Those feelings are almost certainly heightened when the user engaged in risky behavior while under the influence. That’s true whether it’s ketamine or alcohol or Adderall.

There’s a lawsuit playing out and now, potential criminal charges. Regardless, there’s a big lesson to be learned. Don’t do drugs and just stay in school.

The university’s president also apologized for “the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024" and said he was “appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community.”

Actual Article Body:
A former Cornell University student’s lawsuit has kicked up a nationwide furor over the institution’s handling of her allegation that she was raped in a fraternity house two years ago. The alleged victim, known as Jane Doe, claims in her suit that she was sexually assaulted by seven men in the Chi Phi fraternity house, where she was also pressured to consume drugs. All of the men have denied the accusations.

The Tompkins County district attorney announced that he would reopen a criminal investigation into the matter, and much national scrutiny has focused on whether Cornell had shared enough information with law enforcement. At the time, the university expelled two of the alleged perpetrators and punished the remaining five in less severe ways. The university has disputed the notion that it mishandled the case.

Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York, a Democrat, has appointed the state’s attorney general, Letitia James, to investigate Cornell’s handling of the incident. “I am deeply disturbed by Cornell University’s police and how they handled this,” Hochul said in a news conference.

Or subscribe now to read with unlimited access for as low as $10/month.

A free account provides you access to a limited number of free articles each month, plus newsletters, job postings, salary data, and exclusive store discounts.

Cornell University announced Tuesday that it’s suspending all parties and social events held by fraternity chapters through the end of the academic year as it studies “whether and how [fraternity life] can safely continue.” The announcement came in a campus message by President Michael I. Kotlikoff, who also apologized for “the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024" and said he was “appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community.”

Along with the ban on parties, Kotlikoff wrote that Cornell would add staff to its office that receives reports of sexual misconduct, and that it would allow “experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators” from the New York State Police to investigate reports of campus sexual assault, among other steps.

The Ithaca city council voted Wednesday to demand that the Cornell University Police Department refer sex and violent crime investigations to the local police department after it was not looped into the Jane Doe case. The university police department has fallen under scrutiny for not providing a full transcript of its interview with Jane Doe to prosecutors, who declined to pursue a case against the men involved (the local district attorney’s office is also facing criticism for declining to review additional evidence from campus police).

Local officials also voted to temporarily stop issuing city event permits to affiliated student groups — like fraternities — “due to public-safety concerns.” The pause would end November 5.

One of the seven men accused in the Jane Doe case is calling for New York’s attorney general, Letitia James, to be removed from the investigation, saying she “demonstrated a bias and presumption of guilt” on social media.

The lawyer for Gillio Lopes asked a court to remove James as special prosecutor; Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York appointed James, a fellow Democrat, to that post last week.

“What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers,” James wrote on X September 28, days before Hochul tasked her with the investigation. “To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.”

Last week, Cornell University released a statement saying the men accused of sexually assaulting Jane Doe didn’t just have to write essays addressing their conduct, responding to a rumor that had been floating around online. But reflection papers are a common tool in student discipline, I reported in an article. Sometimes, they’re assigned as a condition for suspended students to come back to campus. Other times, they’re a feature of restorative-justice proceedings. But experts told me that in cases of sexual assault, essays would never be enough by themselves.

The proposed no-confidence vote in Cornell administrators wouldn’t be put to a vote until the end of October, the resolution’s leading sponsor told The Chronicle.

Paul Ortiz, a professor of labor history, is slated to present the resolution at the Faculty Senate’s October 14 meeting, at which it’ll be open for discussion. But Ortiz said the voting process won’t begin until after the October 28 meeting, where he’ll reintroduce the resolution. Senators will vote online; Ortiz said ballots are typically open for about a week, meaning results likely won’t be available until early November.

Ten faculty co-sponsors are joining Ortiz on the resolution, which as drafted states that the Senate “has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault.” Ortiz said the group had been spurred to action by students who feared for their safety.

While CNN cited Ortiz as saying that approximately 40 of 75 faculty senators favored the resolution, he told The Chronicle that those numbers were misleading. Those who expressed support, he said, did so while his colleagues were still debating bringing one. And Cornell’s Faculty Senate is larger than he originally stated; The Chronicle counted more than 130 voting members on its website Wednesday.

No-confidence votes are symbolic and don’t hold any inherent power, but Ortiz said bringing his resolution was an important step to take.

“We’ve got to keep this space open where people are talking about this crisis, because it’s an attack on the person and the dignity of the young women and men who are being abused and being assaulted,” he said. “Anyone that wants to sweep that under the rug shouldn’t be employed at a university.”

Two students named in Jane Doe’s lawsuit are still enrolled at Cornell, and faculty members are struggling to teach classes they’re in, CNN reported.

In a Tuesday webinar, the provost said Cornell is working on how to “manage the dynamics” in classrooms that include the two accused students.

An seven-hour sit-in is underway in a Cornell dining hall, “in solidarity with Jane Doe and all survivors of sexual assault and sexual violence,” according to the Cornell Daily Sun. The length of the sit-in corresponds with the amount of time Doe alleges she was assaulted in 2024.

The sit-in is part of a “campus-wide economic blackout” planned by Cornell Black Students United and Cornell NAACP, the student newspaper reported. The organizations are encouraging students to skip classes and avoid spending money on campus today.

In a letter to the University of Arizona’s Greek-life organizations, the dean of students announced she was placing the institution’s 21 interfraternity council chapters on interim activities suspension amid ongoing reports of conduct-code violations.

The dean, Chrissy Lieberman, seemed to nod to Cornell in her letter: The “value of the Greek experience is under scrutiny nationwide.” According to the university’s fall of 2025 data, 12.8 percent of undergraduates at Arizona are involved in Greek life.

Several Arizona fraternities found responsible last spring for misconduct — including hazing, physical assault, and substance-use violations — were already on disciplinary status, and the university warned it would not tolerate further bad behavior. But reports have continued to stream in this fall about harmful conduct within the system.

Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, told faculty and staff members in a Tuesday virtual meeting that he hoped the institution would “become a model for what it looks like to change culture,” according to The New York Times.

He also said while the alleged sexual assault was “horrific,” shutting down fraternities, as some activists have demanded, could send issues “into the shadows.”

Faculty and staff members quoted by the Times said they were frustrated by the “town hall” session, in which they said Kotlikoff and other administrators read prepared statements and answered pre-screened questions.

Cornell University’s Board of Trustees has retained a former Department of Justice official to review its handling of the Jane Doe sexual-assault case. The probe will seek to determine if the university followed procedures in its response to the complaint, the board announced in a statement.

The review will be led by Sally Q. Yates, who served as the U.S. deputy attorney general during the Obama administration. The review will assess the university’s student hearings, disciplinary decisions, response of campus police, campus safety reporting, and coordination with law enforcement.

“The questions raised by the Jane Doe matter warrant a rigorous examination of Cornell’s response to that case, but our responsibility is broader,” Anne Meinig Smalling, a Cornell trustee, said in the statement. “We have asked Ms. Yates and her team to examine Cornell’s overall approach to preventing and responding to sexual misconduct, identify where we are doing things well and where we can do better, and recommend changes that will help make our community safer.”

Members of Cornell’s Faculty Senate have written up a resolution for a vote of no confidence in the administration over its response to fraternity gang-rape allegations, CNN is reporting. A committee will review the resolution and the senate will consider it when it next meets on October 14.

Cornell community members gathered en masse at Ho Plaza on Monday to protest the university’s handling of a sexual-assault case from 2024. Demonstrators demanded all of the men involved be expelled — several were, while others received lighter punishments — and that Cornell ban fraternities. They also called on President Michael Kotlikoff to resign.

A key frustration is how Cornell has punished students protesting the war in Gaza. Cornell suspended some for disruptive conduct in protests, putting international students’ visa statuses at risk.

Activists vandalized a Cornell University administrative building over the university’s handling of Jane Doe’s gang-rape allegations early Monday morning, The Washington Post reported. The spray-painted messages said, “At Cornell rapists are protected protestors are expelled,” and, “Smash the patriarchy.” Several windows have also been shattered.

“We understand the frustration and strong emotions being expressed across our community. Those concerns deserve to be heard, but damaging property is not the answer.” a Cornell spokesman, Kyle Kimball, said. The vandalism comes ahead of a campus protest planned for Monday afternoon.

Summaries of the disciplinary measures taken against the men accused in the Cornell rape case confirm a claim in Jane Doe’s lawsuit that two of the seven were expelled. According to the records, obtained by The New York Times, one man — who had graduated by the time of a disciplinary panel’s ruling — was barred from campus for three years, two were suspended, and two received lighter punishments, including to study sexual harassment and write reflection papers.

Cornell University police officers arrested an individual for drug use at the Chi Phi house less than a day before Jane Doe alleges she was sexually assaulted, according to crime logs analyzed by The Cornell Daily Sun. The university did not place the fraternity on interim suspension in the immediate aftermath of the arrest, but did when Jane Doe filed a complaint weeks later.

Cornell University’s president spoke publicly Saturday in an eight-minute video about the explosive public response to Jane Doe’s gang-rape allegations, saying, “This will not be a moment that passes.”

Michael I. Kotlikoff — who was interim president when Doe reported that she’d been sexually assaulted, and became permanent president in March 2025 — said Doe’s case “raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization, and aspects of party culture and alcohol and drug use.”

Kotlikoff said Cornell officials wouldn’t wait for the forthcoming criminal investigation to improve prevention and response at the university. He said a campus task force’s recommendations for change, finalized in March, were already being carried out.

The president also said Cornell would, further down the line, engage the campus community on broader questions about culture, including “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life.” He said he wanted to preserve the positive aspects of Greek-life organizations while strengthening accountability for individual wrongdoing.

Various laws prevent universities from being fully transparent about how they handle sexual-assault cases, Kotlikoff said, but he said Cornell “will make a greater effort to explain what we can.”

Cornell University’s police department offered additional evidence to the local district attorney about Jane Doe’s rape allegations beyond a condensed six-page statement, but the Tompkins County office declined to review it, The New York Times reports.

The revelation comes as both the university and the district attorney are being questioned over how they handled Doe’s allegations in 2024. The university police statement provided to the district attorney — a summary based on an hours-long interview with Doe — omitted some of Doe’s strongest language, including, “I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped.”

But the new reporting in the Times, citing records it obtained, suggests that the campus police department had conducted additional interviews and alerted the district attorney’s office to that fact.

In comments Friday, President Trump said he felt badly for whomever special prosecutor Letitia James investigated in the Cornell case, “because they won’t get a fair shake.” Trump has long criticized James, the attorney general of New York, in a feud that began with her scrutiny of his business dealings.

Momentum is building for the New York State Legislature to change a part of the law that makes it difficult to prosecute rape cases in which the accuser chooses to drink or use drugs, as the victim in the Cornell case apparently had. The governor of New York, Kathy Hochul, also called for this change on Friday, writing on X, “Choosing to have a drink is not consent, and it’s never a license for sexual assault.”

The Cornell Daily Sun reports that the university has edited its FAQ page about its handling of the gang-rape incident to state that “the victim’s sworn statement and the Snapchat screenshot were shared” with the district attorney’s office, referring to a photo of a Snapchat conversation that appears to show fraternity members referencing Jane Doe in crude terms. The old version of the page had stated that “all investigatory information” had been shared with the district attorney.

That apparent edit comes after The New York Times reported that a signed statement the university had shared with the district attorney omitted some information, including the statement, “I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped.”

All 22 chapter presidents within Cornell’s Interfraternity Council voted to cancel their social events this weekend, according to reporting by The Cornell Daily Sun. The mayor of Ithaca earlier this week called for a pause on all student-event permits as a result of the university’s “appalling response” to the Chi Phi rape allegations.

The controversy that has encircled Cornell represents a stark leadership test for its president, Michael Kotlikoff, as I reported earlier this week. On Kotlikoff’s watch, Cornell made a controversial deal with the Trump administration to restore federal funding. And this spring, the president bumped a protester with his car as he backed out of a parking space. A video of the interaction went viral, prompting a university investigation, which cleared Kotlikoff of wrongdoing.

At a public meeting convened by Cornell’s student government Thursday night, students criticized administrators and shared their own experiences with sexual assault, The New York Times reported. “We’re absolutely ashamed of the events that happened on campus,” said the student body president, Eeshaan Chaudhuri.

Cornell University has banned all fraternity parties in the wake of serious gang-rape allegations by a former female student.

The announcement comes after a former student, refered to in documents as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit accusing seven men from Chi Phi of raping her and plying her with copious amounts of drugs at a 2024 Hawaiian themed party.

She alleged that the sexual assault lasted for seven hours straight, starting around 11pm and continuing until around 5.45am the next day.

Michael I Kotlikoff, the president of Cornell, said: 'We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action.

'Cornell must be a place where safety is not an open question.'

Alongside the party ban, Cornell announced that it will be adding experienced sexual assault investigators to its police force. Accusations continue to mount over whether the internal investigation into the alleged assault went far enough.

Jane Doe's attorney Thomas Giuffra spoke to the Daily Mail following the announcement of the ban. Giuffra stated 'Ms.Doe's goal in filing her lawsuit was not solely for herself.'

The accused men are Matthew Ingalls, Jonathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar.

None of the seven men have been charged with a crime. They all deny any wrongdoing.

In a written statement to Cornell police, Doe said she had arrived at the fraternity house after taking several shots of alcohol with her sorority sisters and getting a mixed drink at a bar in downtown Ithaca, New York.

Bar staff had marked her hand to signify she was under the age of 21, but Doe claimed she was still able to order a mixed drink with approximately two shots of alcohol. The bar has since denied any wrongdoing.

In today's statement Michael I Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, also announced that the Ivy League institution would bring on 'experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators' to review allegations of sexual assault on campus

The consequences of Jane Doe's suit are tangible, social media has been set alight with numerous messages of support and promises to keep her anonymity intact.

Actual Article Body:
Editor’s note: This article discusses mature themes.

We’re wasting an awful lot of time talking about “consent” and sexual regret right now, thanks to a young woman suing several men she had group sex with at Cornell University, when we really should be talking about the powerful effect of not consuming hard drugs.

TMZ this week published newly revealed text messages between who we now know as Cornell’s “Jane Doe” and one of the Chi Phi fraternity members she accused of gang raping her two years ago. “[I]f you have any regrets or anything you want to talk about i am always here to talk about it cause that was a lot,” Doe wrote in one of the messages. “i really do love u and matt and i promise i wont get quiet and weird w u like i did last time.” The name Matt appears to be a reference to another one of the men she is accusing, though public evidence shows she justified and defended their sexual engagement in a similar message to him as well.

And here’s the truly relevant message she sent to one of the accused, as reported by TMZ: “ps. i’m not sure if u remember but i did ket off your d–k at some point?” she wrote. “[A]nd i honestly think that was one of the most insane/jaw dropping moments of the night.” Her use of the word “ket” is apparently a reference to the drug ketamine, which her own lawsuit indicates she snorted an alarming amount of on the night in question.

That brings us to where we should have been all along. College students, ladies in particular, don’t do hard drugs. Especially when it involves a group of men.

We don’t know yet what exactly happened in October 2024 at the Chi Phi fraternity house with Jane Doe. We probably never will. But all public evidence currently indicates a 20-year-old woman got drunk at a sorority house, went to a couple of bars, then went to a frat house where she met a male friend and initially agreed to a threesome that ultimately included drugs and may have included other men.

No one begrudges a college student, whether male or female, drinking underage. If she’s legally old enough to have died for her country, she can have as many drinks as she wants (so long as she’s not caught). But drinking comes with consequences. Everything does. That includes consuming hard drugs.

Jane Doe reportedly said in other text messages days after the night of partying that she could only “sleep and cry all day.” Without concluding whether she was raped, that testimony isn’t discernibly different from any person who has done hard drugs and is on a come-down. Drugs like ketamine create a hyper sense of euphoria while it’s in the system. And once it’s gone, the user crashes. Depression and anxiety are normal. Those feelings are almost certainly heightened when the user engaged in risky behavior while under the influence. That’s true whether it’s ketamine or alcohol or Adderall.

There’s a lawsuit playing out and now, potential criminal charges. Regardless, there’s a big lesson to be learned. Don’t do drugs and just stay in school.
